title: Room and Choir
premise: Lena Dravenmoor, a property surveyor with fifteen years of rationalizing the unexplained, arrives at Hollowmere House to appraise it and finds the building measuring rooms that do not exist. The village's church bell — melted down in 1911 — rings each dusk, and those who hear the whole song are compelled to sing along and vanish into the house's expanding walls. Lena discovers the bell's last verse was never written down: it is the testimony of villagers drowned in 1911 to silence a murder inquiry, and the house keeps them singing until someone hears the truth. To survive the harvest moon, Lena must learn the final verse by listening without joining in — an act of witness the house has never permitted — and speak the drowned villagers' names aloud, freeing them and collapsing Hollowmere into the ordinary, empty ruin it always pretended to be, though Lena leaves forever changed, hearing faint harmonies in every quiet room.
about_author: Oscar Pemberton is the pen name of a former rural planning officer who spent a decade surveying listed buildings across the English fenlands. Their fiction blends bureaucratic precision with folk horror, and they claim every house they have ever appraised has kept at least one secret from them.

chapters.title: The Measurements Do Not Agree
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Arriving at Hollowmere House, Lena's laser measure returns impossible figures: corridors longer outside than in, a staircase to a floor the plans deny. The emotional beat is professional unease curdling into the old, familiar dread Lena has spent fifteen years suppressing.

chapters.title: A Bell That Was Melted Down
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At dusk a bell tolls; the parish records confirm it was sold for scrap in 1911. Villagers go indoors at the sound without being asked. The beat is isolation — Lena realizes no one will discuss the bell, and the house's rooms have shifted overnight.

chapters.title: The Previous Surveyor
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, with found documents. Lena finds the 1998 survey of the same house, unfinished, its author's handwriting deteriorating into song lyrics mid-sentence. The emotional beat is horror at recognizing one's own trade used as bait — the house lures people who measure things.

chapters.title: Choir of the Drowned
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Following the bell into the flooded cellar, Lena sees figures standing in water that shouldn't be there, mouths moving in unison. One breaks formation to look at her. The beat is terror mixed with recognition: the drowned are waiting for something, not hunting.

chapters.title: What the Village Agreed To
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, interleaved with 1911 diary entries. In the archive, Lena learns the village drowned a bell-ringer's family to bury evidence of a landlord's murder, then melted the bell to destroy the witness. The beat is cold anger — the horror is human, and the house remembers it.

chapters.title: The Verse Without Words
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The bell rings a melody with a gap at its end — the unwritten last verse. Lena hums involuntarily and a door in the house opens that was never there, showing a room that is Lena's own childhood bedroom. The beat is violation: the house is learning her.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Knock
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Villagers arrive at Hollowmere, polite and wrong, urging Lena to 'hear the whole song before the moon.' Their leader is the descendant of the 1911 ringleaders, sustaining the house with complicity. The beat is the theme of power's corruption — the village feeds its own guilt to the bell.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Trapped as the house seals its exits, Lena confronts the memory the noises have always echoed: a night fifteen years ago Lena survived something by staying silent. The beat is reckoning — Lena's survival and the village's are the same sin, silence purchased at others' cost.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Rises
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Under the full moon the bell rings the song entire, and the house pulls Lena toward the choir to complete it. Instead Lena stands in the flooded cellar and listens — truly listens — to the final verse, the drowned testimony, without singing. The beat is the climax: witness as resistance, the one act the house cannot digest.

chapters.title: Last Verse, Spoken Aloud
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena speaks the drowned villagers' names into the silence after the song. The bell cracks, the choir releases, and Hollowmere collapses into a mundane ruin with honest measurements. The beat is bittersweet resolution: justice outside the law is done, but Lena walks out carrying harmonies that will never fully stop.
